update.x: I just made an update to my blog about my trip to Rome.

upheaval.x: Since that upheaval Wales have won just once in seven games, beating Northern Ireland in the Nations Cup last May.

uphold.e: From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- + hold. Compare Dutch ophouden (“to stop, cease, hold up”), German aufhalten (“to stop, halt, detain”).
uphold.x: A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit.

upholsterer.e: From upholster + -er, from Middle English upholdester, upholster, from Middle English upholder (“dealer in small goods”), from upholden (“to repair, uphold”).

upholstery.e: First recorded in 1597; from upholster (noun) or upholster(er) + -(er)y or -y.

upload.x: You will have to convert your photograph to a jpg format if you wish to upload it.

upright.e: From Middle English upright, uppryght, upriht, from Old English upriht (“upright; erect”), from Proto-Germanic *upprehtaz, equivalent to up- + right.
upright.x: Supported by pillows, ſhe ſat almoſt upright.

uproar.e: Calque of Dutch oproer or German Aufruhr, as up + roar.

uproot.e: PIE word *wréh₂ds From up- (prefix indicating a higher direction or position) + root (“to tear up by the roots; (figuratively) to remove forcibly from a place.

upsilon.e: From Ancient Greek ὖ ψιλόν (û psilón, “simple Υ”).

upstart.e: From Middle English upstarten, upsterten, equivalent to up- + start.

upstream.x: Input entry is upstream of input validation in the runtime process.

upwards.e: From Middle English upwardes, from Old English upweardes, equivalent to up + -wards. Cognate with Dutch opwaarts (“upwards”), German aufwärts (“upwards”).
upwards.x: The balloon drifted upwards into the sky.

uranium.x: Incorrigible Quid-nuncs, / We would see what would come / Of pelting heaven with chunks / Of crude uranium.

urbane.e: A variant of urban + -ane (a variant of -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives)).
urbane.x: We took advantage of our acquaintance with the urbane Frenchman to join his party; the conversation turned almost entirely on literary subjects.

urchin.e: From Middle English yrchoun, irchoun (“hedgehog; sea urchin”), from Old Northern French irechon, from Vulgar Latin *ērīciōnem, from Latin ērīcius.
urchin.x: And the urchins that stand with their thievish eyes / Forever on watch ran off each with a prize.

urethra.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek οὐρήθρα (ourḗthra, “the passage for urine”), from οὐρέω (ouréō, “to make water”). Recorded in English since 1634.

urgency.x: I have this sudden urgency to use the toilet.

urgently.x: We all urgently need to apply solutions to the problem of pollution.

urinal.e: From Middle English urinal, urynal, orynal, from Old French urinal, orinal (“vessel for urination”), from Latin ūrīnālis (“urinary”).

urinate.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin urinātus, perfect passive participle of urinō (“urinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), equivalent to urine + -ate.
urinate.x: Our new puppy still urinates on the carpet, but we're housebreaking her.

urine.e: From Middle English uryne, from Latin ūrīna (“urine”), from Proto-Indo-European *uh₁r-, zero grade of *woh₁-r̥ (“water, liquid, milk”).

urticaria.e: Borrowed from New Latin urtīcāria, from Latin urtīca (“nettle”) + -āria.

usable.e: From Old French usable, from the verb user (“to use”).

usage.x: In descriptive fact, word senses are established by usage.

usefulness.x: The usefulness of his latest reorganisation has been disputed.

username.x: His username and password on his Apple PC is VolvestarcXXX.

usher.e: From Middle English ussher, uscher, usscher, from Anglo-Norman usser and Old French ussier, uissier (“porter, doorman”) (compare French huissier), from Vulgar Latin…

usufruct.e: From Late Latin ūsufrūctus, from ūsus + frūctus (“usage of the fruits of production”).

usurer.e: Anglo-Norman, from Old French usurier, Latin ūsūra (“interest”).
usurer.x: Profitless usurer, why dost thou use So great a sum of sums, yet canst not live?

usurp.e: From Middle English usurpen, from Old French usurper, from Latin ūsūrpō.
usurp.x: Most Republicans in Congress are complying as Mr. Trump usurps the power of the national legislature, as laid out in Article 1 of the Constitution.

usurpation.e: From Middle English usurpacioun, from Old French usurpacion, from Latin ūsurpātiō; equivalent to usurp + -ation.

usurper.e: From Middle English usurper, usurpour, usurpur, from Middle French usurpeur; equivalent to usurp + -er.

usury.e: From Middle English usurie, from Latin ūsūria, from ūsūra (“lending at interest, usury”) from ūsus (“use”), from stem of ūtī (“to use”). Compare usurp and use.
usury.x: As a practical matter, California usury laws do not seriously inconvenience most lenders, and offer little protection to most borrowers.

utensil.e: From Middle English utensyl, from Old French utensile, from Latin ūtēnsilis (“useful, usable”).
utensil.x: We have convenient storage for all the kitchen/eating utensils.

uterine.e: From Middle French utérin, from Latin uterinus (“pertaining to the womb; born of the same mother”), from Latin uterus (“womb”). Related to English uterus.

utilise.e: From French utiliser, from Italian utilizzare, from utile (“useful”), from Latin ūtilis, from ūtī (“use”). Attested c. 1810.

utility.e: From Middle English utilite, from Old French utilite, utilitet (“usefulness”), from Latin ūtilitās, from uti (“to use”). By surface analysis, utile + -ity.
utility.x: "The profession has its utility, but I should be sorry to see any friend of mine belonging to it."

utter.e: PIE word *úd The adjective is derived from Middle English outre, utter, uttre (“situated on the outside of, exterior”), from Old English ūtera (“exterior, outer”…
utter.x: And ſhould Gods eare, / VVhich needs not man, be ty'd to thoſe / VVho heare not him, but quickly heare / His utter foes?

utterance.e: From Middle English utteraunce, outeraunce; equivalent to utter + -ance.
